HazardWeaver: Scientific Route Selection
for Hazard Analysis Agents

 

Wangshu Zhu1  Xueqi Cheng1  Liang Wu2  Yushun Dong1

1Department of Computer Science, Florida State University   2Nokia

{wz26b,xc25,yushun.dong}@fsu.edu    liang.wu@nokia.com

Abstract

Understanding and assessing natural hazards is essential for disaster preparedness and risk reduction. Recent advances in large language models have spurred growing interest in AI agents for hazard analysis, particularly their ability to integrate scientific data, models, and tools into automated workflows. However, effective automation requires agents to determine which scientific methods are appropriate for a given event and executable with the available data and tools. As new evidence and execution results become available, these conditions can change, requiring agents to reconsider their choices. We formulate this problem as state-dependent scientific route selection and introduce HazardWeaver. Specifically, HazardWeaver first leverages the Hazard Knowledge Compiler to extract evidence-linked conditions governing scientific applicability, then its Hazard Capability Graph represents executable scientific capabilities and checks compatibility between their inputs and outputs. Using these complementary representations, the Hazard Weaver Agent component selects applicable and executable routes, carries out their workflows, and revises its decisions as the analysis state changes. To evaluate both the scientific outputs and the decisions that produce them, we introduce the Hazard Weaver Benchmark, comprising 141 instances across seven single-hazard domains and four multi-hazard interaction classes. The benchmark accommodates multiple valid scientific routes and evaluates output correctness, route validity, and justified abstention. Extensive experiments on this benchmark show that HazardWeaver outperforms existing agent systems, with the largest gains on tasks with multiple eligible scientific routes. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/LabRAI/HazardWeaver.

1 Introduction

Natural-hazard analysis supports disaster preparedness and risk reduction. The same target can often be reached through several scientific routes. Wildfire spread, flood extent, and earthquake source parameters, for example, can each be estimated through empirical, physical, statistical, or learned methods, which differ in assumptions, required observations, validity ranges, and computational dependencies (Perry, 1998; Huot et al., 2022; Nearing et al., 2024; Zhu and Beroza, 2018; Stewart et al., 2015; Reichstein et al., 2019; Karpatne et al., 2017). A task specification alone therefore does not fix how it should be analyzed, since scientific evidence determines which routes apply while the available resources determine which routes can currently run. The difficulty grows when multiple hazards occur simultaneously or in cascade, since one hazard alters the conditions under which another must be assessed (Kappes et al., 2012; Gill and Malamud, 2014; Zscheischler et al., 2018; Zscheischler et al., 2020). Recent advances in large language models have spurred growing interest in AI agents that integrate such scientific data, models, and tools into automated workflows (Boiko et al., 2023; Bran et al., 2024; Jaber et al., 2026). On an actual event, however, the evidence and tools an agent depends on can shift as the event unfolds. The agent must therefore repeatedly reconsider which route it can trust and run. Route choice thus becomes a state-dependent decision, which leads to the question we study: given a hazard task and the current analysis state, which scientific route should an agent take?

Existing work provides important components for automated hazard analysis, but two gaps remain in how scientific routes are grounded and revised. Gap 1: Scientific Route Grounding. Hazard models offer established procedures within selected modeling regimes (Finney, 1998; Bates et al., 2010), yet the conditions governing their applicability are scattered across papers, reports, and model documentation. Selecting an appropriate route therefore requires making these conditions explicit and checking them against the available task evidence. This grounding must also extend to how scientific assets are combined. Although workflow and disaster-agent systems expose executable tools and operational pipelines, a route may draw on heterogeneous assets whose outputs and inputs are not directly compatible. These assets must therefore be represented as executable capabilities with explicit applicability conditions and compatibility requirements. Gap 2: State-Dependent Route Selection. Automated experimentation methods, from classical AutoML search (Akiba et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021) to recent LLM-driven data-science agents, optimize models, programs, or workflows for a specified objective. However, this optimization alone does not establish which routes remain scientifically and operationally eligible as execution proceeds. In hazard analysis, new artifacts, unavailable inputs, execution failures, or changing downstream requirements can alter the eligible route set. An agent must therefore reassess route eligibility as the scientific and computational state evolves and revise its decisions accordingly. These requirements also call for route-aware evaluation: because several routes may validly satisfy the same task, evaluation must assess both final-artifact quality and whether route selection, revision, or abstention was justified under the observed state.

To meet these requirements, HazardWeaver integrates scientific grounding, state-dependent route selection, and route-aware evaluation within a unified evidence-to-execution architecture. Scientific route grounding is supported by two complementary components. The Hazard Knowledge Compiler (HKC) derives evidence-linked applicability conditions from scientific literature and resolves them against the task context. The Hazard Capability Graph (HCG) represents hazard models, datasets, formulas, and transformations as typed executable capabilities, connecting them only under a registered compatibility relation. Building on these components, the Hazard Weaver Agent (HWA) determines the eligible route set by combining the applicability conditions from HKC with capability reachability in HCG. It selects and executes a route, then reassesses eligibility and revises its decisions as the state evolves. Within this process, the language model manages route decisions and execution flow, while scientific models and solvers produce the numerical, spatial, and probabilistic outputs. To evaluate both the resulting artifacts and the decisions that produce them, the Hazard Weaver Benchmark (HWB) assesses artifact correctness, route validity at commitment time, and recovery-aware abstention. Specifically, HWB contains 141 sealed instances spanning seven single-hazard domains and four multi-hazard interaction classes. Its construction infrastructure includes a global atlas of 3,062 registered geospatial scenarios, with 542 materialized for benchmark generation (Figure 1).

Contributions.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    A novel scientific-agent decision problem. We formulate hazard analysis as state-dependent scientific route selection, where route eligibility requires both evidence-based scientific applicability and capability reachability, and is updated throughout execution.

  • •

    An evidence-grounded adaptive agent system. We introduce an agent system that compiles evidence into route conditions, connects scientific capabilities through typed compatibility, and updates executable workflows as the analysis state evolves.

  • •

    A globally grounded, route-aware benchmark. HWB comprises 141 instances built from scientific datasets and benchmarks, spans seven single-hazard domains and four multi-hazard interaction classes, and jointly evaluates artifact correctness and route validity.

2 Preliminaries

Let ℋ\mathcal{H} denote the set of hazard settings, each being either a single hazard or a multi-hazard interaction class. For h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H}, let 𝒯h\mathcal{T}_{h} denote its associated scientific tasks and ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} the registered route families for task t∈𝒯ht\in\mathcal{T}_{h}, together forming the design space ℳ={(h,t,r):h∈ℋ,t∈𝒯h,r∈ℛt}\mathcal{M}=\{(h,t,r):h\in\mathcal{H},\,t\in\mathcal{T}_{h},\,r\in\mathcal{R}_{t}\}. A task instance is q=(h,t,ξ,Γt,cq)q=(h,t,\xi,\Gamma_{t},c_{q}), where ξ\xi is the event and environmental context, Γt\Gamma_{t} specifies the requested output in 𝒴t\mathcal{Y}_{t}, and cqc_{q} is the information cutoff associated with the decision. We denote scientific knowledge by 𝒦\mathcal{K} and executable scientific capabilities by 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

Definition 1 (Route family and workflow).

A route family r∈ℛtr\in\mathcal{R}_{t} specifies a scientific solution structure together with its scientific conditions and required capability signatures. A concrete workflow π∈Inst⁡(r,𝒢)\pi\in\operatorname{Inst}(r;\mathcal{G}) realizes rr by binding its stages to registered datasets, models, formulas, transformations, software, and other capabilities in 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

Definition 2 (Analysis state and trajectory).

At decision step kk, the analysis state is sk=(𝒳k,𝒞k,bk)s_{k}=(\mathcal{X}_{k},\mathcal{C}_{k},b_{k}), where 𝒳k\mathcal{X}_{k} contains available raw and derived artifacts, 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k} records capability availability, and bkb_{k} is the remaining resource budget. An execution trajectory is τ=(s0,a0,s1,…,aK−1,sK)\tau=(s_{0},a_{0},s_{1},\ldots,a_{K-1},s_{K}), and route commitments made along τ\tau are recorded as Commit⁡(τ)={(k,rk)}\operatorname{Commit}(\tau)=\{(k,r_{k})\}.

A route counts as usable at sks_{k} only when it clears two checks: scientific applicability Asci​(r,q,sk,𝒦)A_{\mathrm{sci}}(r,q,s_{k};\mathcal{K}), resolved from the evidence attached to rr, and capability reachability Acap​(r,sk,𝒢)A_{\mathrm{cap}}(r,s_{k};\mathcal{G}), resolved from the executable assets available at sks_{k}; Section 3 details how each operator is computed. The eligible route set at sks_{k} collects exactly the routes passing both checks,

ℛtelig​(q,sk)={r∈ℛt:Asci​(r,q,sk,𝒦)=Applicable∧Acap​(r,sk,𝒢)=Reachable}.\mathcal{R}_{t}^{\mathrm{elig}}(q,s_{k})\;=\;\bigl\{\,r\in\mathcal{R}_{t}\,:\,A_{\mathrm{sci}}(r,q,s_{k};\mathcal{K})=\textsc{Applicable}\ \wedge\ A_{\mathrm{cap}}(r,s_{k};\mathcal{G})=\textsc{Reachable}\,\bigr\}. (1)
Problem 1 (State-Dependent Scientific Route Selection and Execution).

Given (q,s0,𝒦,𝒢,B)(q,s_{0},\mathcal{K},\mathcal{G},B), the goal at every committed step kk is to execute a route rkr_{k} drawn from ℛtelig​(q,sk)\mathcal{R}_{t}^{\mathrm{elig}}(q,s_{k}) (Eq. 1), recomputing this set as sks_{k} evolves with new evidence, artifacts, and capability availability, and returning y∈𝒴ty\in\mathcal{Y}_{t} or abstaining with ⊥\bot once no state reachable within BB still admits one.

3 Methodology

This section develops HazardWeaver, shown in Figure 2, in the order its route decision actually forms. Section 3.1 grounds scientific applicability through HKC, Section 3.2 establishes capability reachability through HCG, Section 3.3 combines both signals in HWA to select, execute, and revise a route, and Section 3.4 evaluates the resulting decisions through HWB.

3.1 Hazard Knowledge Compiler: Scientific Applicability

A scientific route applies only when its assumptions and validity conditions match the task context, evidence that sits scattered across papers and model documentation. HKC extracts a structured condition set from its current literature corpus and checks it against the available task evidence. Retrieval-augmented methods provide relevant context (Lewis et al., 2020), while scientific information extraction provides representations of entities and relations (Luan et al., 2018; Jain et al., 2020).

Evidence-Grounded Condition Extraction. For each route family rr, HKC retrieves this evidence, maps it into a common schema, and canonicalizes equivalent entities into a condition set 𝒦r={κ1,…,κmr}\mathcal{K}_{r}=\{\kappa_{1},\ldots,\kappa_{m_{r}}\}, where each κi\kappa_{i} records a proposition’s semantic role, applicable scope, logical direction, and supporting source, spanning route assumptions, required observations, validity ranges, scale, uncertainty, and known failure conditions. Condition-Level Applicability. At task time, HKC relates each required condition κi∈𝒦rreq\kappa_{i}\in\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{req}}_{r} to the evidence available in ξ\xi and sks_{k}, assigns zi​(q,sk)∈Satisfied,Violated,Unresolvedz_{i}(q,s_{k})\in{\textsc{Satisfied},\textsc{Violated},\textsc{Unresolved}}, and derives route-level applicability:

Asci(r,q,sk;𝒦)={Applicable,zi(q,sk)=Satisfied,∀κi∈𝒦reqr,Inapplicable,∃κi∈𝒦rreq:zi​(q,sk)=Violated,Undetermined,otherwise.A_{\mathrm{sci}}(r,q,s_{k};\mathcal{K})=\begin{cases}\textsc{Applicable},&z_{i}(q,s_{k})=\textsc{Satisfied},\ \forall\kappa_{i}\in\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{req}}_{r},\\ \textsc{Inapplicable},&\exists\,\kappa_{i}\in\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{req}}_{r}:z_{i}(q,s_{k})=\textsc{Violated},\\ \textsc{Undetermined},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (2)

The task target and information cutoff remain fixed; condition status is recomputed from evidence available in the current state. Applicability is thus grounded in individual condition status, each carrying its own provenance and task evidence, so an unresolved or changed condition can revise the route decision without reconstructing the rest of the record; an Undetermined condition keeps rr outside the eligible set (Eq. 1) without discarding it, since HWA can request the missing evidence during recovery (Section 3.3) and re-resolve AsciA_{\mathrm{sci}} once new context arrives.

3.2 Hazard Capability Graph: Scientific Capability Composition

Scientific applicability does not guarantee executability, since an appropriate route can still require unavailable capabilities or produce artifacts that no downstream model can consume. Analysis-readiness specifications motivate explicit scientific metadata (Baumann, 2024), and semantic workflow systems support composition under component constraints (Gil et al., 2011). HCG represents the available scientific ecosystem as a typed directed graph 𝒢=(𝒱G,ℰG)\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V}_{G},\mathcal{E}_{G}) and checks whether a route’s required capabilities are actually reachable in the current state.

Typed Capability Composition. Nodes in 𝒢\mathcal{G} are executable capabilities, each recording its entry point, scientific function, dependencies, validation metadata, provenance, and typed input and output ports of type α=(v,u,f,Ωx,Ωt,δ,σ,p)\alpha=(v,u,f,\Omega_{x},\Omega_{t},\delta,\sigma,p), and edges are valid artifact transfers: for a produced artifact of type α′\alpha^{\prime} and a required input type α\alpha, a direct connection is permitted only when

α′⊧α⟺⋀j=18α′j∼jαj.\alpha^{\prime}\models\alpha\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad{\textstyle\bigwedge_{j=1}^{8}}\alpha^{\prime}_{j}\sim_{j}\alpha_{j}. (3)

where ∼j\sim_{j} is the registered compatibility relation for field jj; exact agreement and representation-preserving conversions satisfy this directly, while information-changing operations such as aggregation, interpolation, learned downscaling, and thresholding remain explicit graph capabilities, so their effects stay visible in the workflow’s provenance. State-Dependent Capability Reachability. Given route family rr and state sks_{k}, HCG searches for workflow realizations Inst⁡(r,𝒢,sk)\operatorname{Inst}(r;\mathcal{G},s_{k}) whose required capabilities are available and whose adjacent artifacts satisfy Eq. 3, giving capability reachability

Acap​(r,sk,𝒢)={Reachable,Inst⁡(r,𝒢,sk)≠∅,Unavailable,Inst⁡(r,𝒢,sk)=∅​ under the known state,Undetermined,capability information is incomplete.A_{\mathrm{cap}}(r,s_{k};\mathcal{G})=\begin{cases}\textsc{Reachable},&\operatorname{Inst}(r;\mathcal{G},s_{k})\neq\varnothing,\\ \textsc{Unavailable},&\operatorname{Inst}(r;\mathcal{G},s_{k})=\varnothing\text{ under the known state},\\ \textsc{Undetermined},&\text{capability information is incomplete}.\end{cases} (4)

As with AsciA_{\mathrm{sci}}, an Undetermined status keeps rr outside the eligible set without discarding it. When capability availability or an artifact changes, HCG searches for a compatible replacement subpath or prompts HWA to reconsider the route when it does not.

Provenance records connect each derived artifact to the capabilities and inputs that produced it, following the purpose of interoperable workflow provenance (Khan et al., 2019). The illustrated scientific assets include an Earth-observation foundation model (Jakubik et al., 2023) and WEST, a postfire debris-flow volume model (Gorr et al., 2026). A spatial flow-path artifact requires a separate downstream capability in addition to a volume estimate.

3.3 Hazard Weaver Agent: Adaptive Route Selection

HWA operationalizes Eq. 1 at every decision step, turning the intersection of scientific applicability and capability reachability into an executed, revisable route commitment.

Model-Backed Route Execution. At state sks_{k}, ℛtelig​(q,sk)\mathcal{R}_{t}^{\mathrm{elig}}(q,s_{k}) combines AsciA_{\mathrm{sci}} from HKC with AcapA_{\mathrm{cap}} from HCG, which exclude routes for different reasons, conflicting scientific requirements versus requirements that cannot currently be realized, letting HWA trace an excluded route to its specific cause and target the matching recovery operation. For every rr in this set, HWA receives its grounded conditions, workflow realizations, provenance, uncertainty, and resource requirements, and a language-model policy selects rk∼μθ(⋅∣q,sk,ℛtelig(q,sk))r_{k}\sim\mu_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q,s_{k},\mathcal{R}_{t}^{\mathrm{elig}}(q,s_{k})), records the commitment (k,rk)(k,r_{k}), instantiates π(k)∈Inst⁡(rk,𝒢,sk)\pi^{(k)}\in\operatorname{Inst}(r_{k};\mathcal{G},s_{k}), and executes its capabilities; the language model controls only the route decision and execution flow, while the executed models, solvers, formulas, and transformations produce the numerical, spatial, and probabilistic outputs, keeping the terminal artifact linked through provenance to the route that produced it. Revisable Route Commitments. Execution can reveal missing inputs, alter capability availability, or invalidate downstream compatibility, so HWA updates sks_{k} and recomputes Eq. 1 after every step: a route that remains eligible continues with its current or repaired workflow, and one that does not sends the policy back to the updated eligible set. When this set is empty, HWA explores permitted recovery operations, information requests, compatible transformations, capability substitutions, and alternative realizations, over the states Rec⁡(sk,bk)\operatorname{Rec}(s_{k},b_{k}) reachable within the remaining budget, and uses the recovery outcome to decide whether to abstain. Here Rec⁡(sk,bk)\operatorname{Rec}(s_{k},b_{k}) is the budget-bounded reachable closure over the finite set of grounded actions permitted for the instance. The implemented search explores this closure within its budget. Failure to find a route is not a formal proof that no feasible route exists.

3.4 Hazard Weaver Benchmark: Route-Aware Evaluation

A task may admit several valid routes, and the valid set may shift as conditions or capabilities change, so artifact correctness alone cannot certify a valid decision. We therefore introduce the Hazard Weaver Benchmark (HWB), which evaluates the final artifact together with the route and execution state that produced it. HWB derives tasks with explicit output contracts from established scientific datasets, operational products, and benchmarks, and constructs candidate routes from evidence-grounded Route Cards and registered capabilities. Instances are admitted only after provenance, temporal-cutoff, and replay checks, after which the inventory, route registry, and task-specific evaluators are sealed; benchmark-side references and route judgments remain hidden from the solver. Appendix A and Appendix C detail the construction and evaluation protocol.

Benchmark-Side Route Validity. Using hidden scientific conditions and benchmark-side capability state kept outside solver context, HWB constructs ℛtelig,B​(q,sk)\mathcal{R}_{t}^{\mathrm{elig},B}(q,s_{k}) by the same criteria as Eqs. 2–4. A trajectory is route-valid when every commitment falls inside this set at its commitment state,

VrouteB(q,τ)=𝟙[rk∈ℛtelig,B(q,sk),∀(k,rk)∈Commit(τ)],V_{\mathrm{route}}^{B}(q,\tau)=\mathbb{1}\left[r_{k}\in\mathcal{R}_{t}^{\mathrm{elig},B}(q,s_{k}),\;\forall(k,r_{k})\in\operatorname{Commit}(\tau)\right], (5)

crediting any route the benchmark itself registers as valid without requiring the agent to reproduce the construction-time witness workflow. Writing θ⁡(x)\theta(x) for a raw artifact’s information time and Src⁡(z)\operatorname{Src}(z) for the raw-source ancestors of derived artifact zz, temporal validity requires every such ancestor to have been available by the cutoff cqc_{q},

Vcausal(q,τ)=𝟙[θ(x)≤cq,∀x∈⋃z∈Used⁡(τ)Src(z)],V_{\mathrm{causal}}(q,\tau)=\mathbb{1}\Big[\theta(x)\leq c_{q},\ \forall x\in{\textstyle\bigcup_{z\in\operatorname{Used}(\tau)}}\operatorname{Src}(z)\Big], (6)

so a derived artifact may be computed after cqc_{q} once all its sources were available in time. Together with Vtype​(τ)V_{\mathrm{type}}(\tau) from Eq. 3, provenance validity Vprov​(y,τ)V_{\mathrm{prov}}(y,\tau) linking the terminal artifact to an executed route commitment, and budget validity Vbudget​(τ,B)V_{\mathrm{budget}}(\tau;B), these give joint execution validity Vexec​(q,τ,B)=Vtype​(τ)⋅Vcausal​(q,τ)⋅Vbudget​(τ,B)V_{\mathrm{exec}}(q,\tau;B)=V_{\mathrm{type}}(\tau)\cdot V_{\mathrm{causal}}(q,\tau)\cdot V_{\mathrm{budget}}(\tau;B). The benchmark contract accepts abstention only when permitted recovery cannot reach another registered benchmark-valid route,

VabsB(q,sk,bk)=𝟙[⋃s′∈Rec⁡(sk,bk)ℛtelig,B(q,s′)=∅],V_{\mathrm{abs}}^{B}(q,s_{k},b_{k})=\mathbb{1}\Big[{\textstyle\bigcup_{s^{\prime}\in\operatorname{Rec}(s_{k},b_{k})}}\mathcal{R}_{t}^{\mathrm{elig},B}(q,s^{\prime})=\varnothing\Big], (7)

which defines the benchmark criterion over its registered recovery transitions. Applying this criterion requires the benchmark to establish the reachable set under those transitions; a solver timeout alone does not establish that no usable route remains.

Decision-Constrained Accuracy. HWB combines artifact correctness with these validity checks into Decision-Constrained Accuracy: writing the solver’s return as o∈𝒴t∪{⊥}o\in\mathcal{Y}_{t}\cup\{\bot\} and Eq​(y)∈{0,1}E_{q}(y)\in\{0,1\} for task-specific artifact success under its native evaluator,

DCA⁡(q,o,τ,B)={Eq​(y)​VrouteB​(q,τ)​Vprov​(y,τ)​Vexec​(q,τ,B),o=y,VabsB​(q,sK,bK)​VrouteB​(q,τ)​Vexec​(q,τ,B),o=⊥,\mathrm{DCA}(q,o,\tau;B)=\begin{cases}E_{q}(y)\,V_{\mathrm{route}}^{B}(q,\tau)\,V_{\mathrm{prov}}(y,\tau)\,V_{\mathrm{exec}}(q,\tau;B),&o=y,\\[3.0pt] V_{\mathrm{abs}}^{B}(q,s_{K},b_{K})\,V_{\mathrm{route}}^{B}(q,\tau)\,V_{\mathrm{exec}}(q,\tau;B),&o=\bot,\end{cases} (8)

aggregated over an evaluation set as DCA⁡(𝒬)=1|𝒬|​∑q∈𝒬DCA⁡(q,oq,τq,B)\mathrm{DCA}(\mathcal{Q})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}|}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}\mathrm{DCA}(q,o_{q},\tau_{q};B); native scientific metrics stay task-specific and are reported separately, so DCA measures decision validity without folding heterogeneous scientific errors into one score. HWB further builds matched interventions that alter one factor governing route choice while holding the rest of the task fixed: evidence relevant to AsciA_{\mathrm{sci}}, availability or compatibility relevant to AcapA_{\mathrm{cap}}, the state after execution begins, or an upstream hazard variable in a registered physical interaction. These interventions test whether route selection, recovery, and the resulting artifacts respond consistently to controlled changes in the route space.

4 Experimental Setup

Benchmark. The primary comparison uses the same 141 sealed HWB instances, HCG capability catalog, and evaluator for all systems. The instances draw on eleven published datasets, operational products, and scientific benchmarks: PWFDF and USGS Ground Failure (King et al., 2025; Allstadt et al., 2022), SFINCS and FloodCastBench (Leijnse et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2025), NOAA CPC SPI (NOAA Climate Prediction Center, 2026), SeisBench (Woollam et al., 2022), ExtremeWeatherBench and NASA LHASA v2 (McGovern et al., 2026; NASA Goddard Earth Sciences Data and Information Services Center, 2025), TCBench and NOAA Storm Events (Gomez et al., 2026; NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, 1996), and WildfireSpreadTS (Gerard et al., 2023). These sources provide observed events, forcing data, and reference outputs used to construct route-selection and execution tasks. The inventory contains 90 single-hazard and 51 multi-hazard instances; 45 admit one route and 96 admit multiple routes. Appendix A defines the tracks and evaluation strata.

Baselines. We compare HazardWeaver with adapted versions of Plan-and-Solve (Wang et al., 2023a), Self-Consistency (Wang et al., 2023b), DisasterBench-ToT (Chen et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2023), MLE-STAR (Nam et al., 2025), AutoML-Agent (Trirat et al., 2025), Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023), AIDE (Jiang et al., 2025), DS-Agent (Guo et al., 2024), R&D-Agent (Yang et al., 2025), and ReAct (Yao et al., 2022). All methods use the same task inventory, policy backbone, route catalog, scientific replay, and evaluator. Appendix E documents the adaptations and implementation details.

Metrics. The primary metric is Decision-Constrained Accuracy (DCA; Eq. 8). We also report artifact validity EqE_{q}, aggregate trajectory validity VqV_{q}, and Macro DCA, which weights the 11 tracks equally. Binomial rates use Wilson 95% confidence intervals (Wilson, 1927).

Implementation. The five ablation backbones are OLMo-3.1-32B, Mixtral-8x22B, Gemma-4-31B-it, Llama-3.3-70B, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. The corresponding model-family reports describe OLMo (Olmo et al., 2026), Mixtral (Jiang et al., 2024), Gemma (Gemma et al., 2026), Llama (Grattafiori et al., 2024), and DeepSeek (Deepseek, 2026). The evaluated variants are listed in Appendix D.

5 Experiments

We evaluate HazardWeaver through three research questions. RQ1: How does HazardWeaver compare with representative agent baselines? RQ2: Which design mechanisms contribute to decision-valid scientific execution? RQ3: How consistently does HazardWeaver perform across language-model backbones and hazard-task settings?

5.1 System Performance

We answer RQ1 by comparing HazardWeaver with adapted agent systems and general control strategies. All methods use the same task inventory, Llama backbone, registered route catalog, and DCA evaluator. Table 1 reports performance across hazard composition and route multiplicity.

The comparison covers two complementary baseline families. AIDE, DS-Agent, R&D-Agent, MLE-STAR, AutoML-Agent, and DisasterBench-ToT adapt representative agent-system designs to the benchmark interface. ReAct, Reflexion, Self-Consistency, and Plan-and-Solve evaluate alternative control strategies with the same backbone and scientific tools as HazardWeaver. HazardWeaver reaches 89.4% overall DCA, compared with 41.1% for the strongest baseline. The difference is most pronounced when several routes are available: Plan-and-Solve performs well with one route but declines sharply under multiple-route choice, while HazardWeaver rises to 93.8%. Iterative refinement, retrieval, search, reflection, and explicit planning therefore provide limited benefit when the controller must identify which scientific workflow is valid. HazardWeaver remains strong across both hazard compositions and route regimes, indicating that its advantage comes from structured route eligibility rather than a particular task subset.

5.2 Component and Mechanism Analysis

RQ2 examines whether HazardWeaver benefits from explicitly representing scientific eligibility and maintaining it as execution proceeds. We test these two design choices separately. The first experiment removes the evidence-linked conditions supplied by HKC or the typed compatibility constraints supplied by HCG. The second disables route updating on the subset of tasks for which eligibility can change during execution.

Scientific constraints. Figure 3 shows the same directional result across all five backbones: Full HazardWeaver outperforms both ablated variants. The effect is strongest for policies that can otherwise execute the selected workflow reliably. On Llama, full DCA reaches 93.8%, while removing HKC conditions or HCG typing reduces it to 45.8% and 47.9%. DeepSeek exhibits the same pattern at a smaller scale. The weaker policies retain less performance overall, but neither ablation improves any backbone. These results distinguish scientific route selection from ordinary tool use. HKC removes routes whose assumptions do not match the task context, while HCG prevents compositions whose inputs and outputs are incompatible. Without either constraint, access to the correct scientific capabilities is insufficient for selecting a valid workflow.

Route updating. Table 2 isolates the second design choice on the 40 benchmark instances where route eligibility may change during execution. Recomputing eligibility improves every backbone, raising pooled DCA from 16.0% to 41.5%. The gain is largest for Llama, whose stronger policy can exploit the revised route set once an earlier workflow becomes ineligible. The consistent direction across all five backbones shows that this benefit does not depend on one model family. A capable controller still requires an up-to-date decision space, since a fixed eligible set retains invalidated routes. Overall, reliable scientific route decisions require evidence-linked applicability conditions, typed capability composition, and continued maintenance of the eligible route set.

5.3 Generalization Across Backbones and Task Structures

RQ3 examines whether HazardWeaver remains effective when its policy model changes and which task structures expose the remaining differences. We hold the benchmark, HKC conditions, HCG capabilities, execution interface, and evaluator fixed, and replace only the language-model backbone.

Cross-backbone effectiveness. Table 3 shows that HazardWeaver remains effective across all five policy backbones, with overall DCA ranging from 60.3% to 89.4%. Llama and DeepSeek achieve the strongest results, while Gemma retains nearly 80% DCA with a smaller model. Macro DCA closely follows the overall ordering, showing that the ranking is balanced by all tracks. The marginal validity rates sharpen this result: artifact validity broadly follows DCA, whereas trajectory validity remains consistently high across backbones. The remaining cross-backbone separation is therefore concentrated in producing the required scientific artifact and selecting the valid scientific route.

Hazard composition. Figure 4(a) shows that the strongest policies preserve most of their performance when tasks move from single-hazard analysis to multi-hazard composition. Llama and DeepSeek remain above 80% on multi-hazard tasks, whereas the gap widens for Mixtral and Gemma. Scientific composition therefore provides a more discriminating test of the policy backbone than isolated hazard analysis, since the agent must carry intermediate state across stages and select a compatible downstream workflow while preserving scientific validity throughout the composed analysis.

Route multiplicity. Figure 4(b) reveals a sharper difference across route regimes. Performance on the one-route subset is tightly grouped across the five backbones, whereas the multiple-route subset produces substantially wider separation. Llama and DeepSeek achieve higher DCA on the multiple-route subset, while the weaker policies exploit the available alternatives less consistently. Route-rich tasks therefore provide the clearest distinction between policy backbones within the same HazardWeaver architecture. This descriptive pattern complements Section 5.2, where controlled ablations establish the contribution of the route-eligibility mechanisms themselves.

Track-level coverage. Figure 4(c) confirms that the aggregate results reflect broad coverage rather than success on one hazard family. The strongest backbones form consistently broad profiles across single- and multi-hazard tracks. Flood remains the clearest shared bottleneck, while compound tracks such as multi-peril impact and earthquake-triggered landslide separate the policy backbones more strongly. These differences identify where future improvements should focus: transferring scientific state across stages and choosing among competing composed workflows.

6 Related Work

Scientific Route Grounding. Hazard science provides specialized empirical, physical, statistical, and learned models for single- and multi-hazard analysis, such as fire-area simulators and inertial shallow-water flood solvers (Finney, 1998; Bates et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2026). These models encode scientific assumptions through equations, required observations, calibration regimes, and validity ranges, while scientific workflow research represents executable operations through interfaces, dependencies, and capability graphs (Ahn et al., 2022; Zhai et al., 2026). DisasterBench evaluates planning under typed tool interfaces (Chen et al., 2026), and DORA extends disaster agents to heterogeneous geospatial and learned tools with expert-authored tasks and replayable trajectories (Wang et al., 2026). These systems establish capable execution environments, but selecting among methods that target the same output also depends on variable definitions, units, spatial and temporal support, resolution, uncertainty, provenance, and operating scale (Baumann, 2024; Lee et al., 2025). Multi-hazard analysis compounds this requirement, since the output of one hazard model becomes an input condition of the next (Kappes et al., 2012). Existing workflow representations capture executable dependencies well, while task-conditioned scientific applicability remains largely external to their route structures. HazardWeaver connects these layers by grounding alternative route families in evidence-linked conditions and composing them through typed executable capabilities.

State-Dependent Route Decision. Automated machine learning formulates estimator and pipeline selection as search over a fixed target and evaluation objective (Akiba et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021). Recent agents extend this process to executable code, iterative experiment refinement, and data-science workflows (Shinn et al., 2023; Trirat et al., 2025; Nam et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2024; Cheng and Dong, 2026), while richer planning systems organize available tools before execution (Liu et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Rana et al., 2023). Hazard analysis additionally requires route eligibility to follow the current scientific state because new evidence, intermediate artifacts, and capability outcomes such as tool failures or missing inputs can change which workflows remain applicable. Related benchmarks evaluate planning, multi-step trajectories, and task outcomes (Valmeekam et al., 2023; Trivedi et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025; Pothuri et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2024; Chan et al., 2024), including compositional and changing environments (Wang et al., 2025; Yoa et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2025), and recent abstention benchmarks study whether agents can recognize when to stop acting (Liu et al., 2026). Route-plural scientific analysis further requires relating an executed workflow to the state in which it was selected while accommodating multiple registered solutions, and judging abstention by whether any usable route remains reachable. HazardWeaver addresses this problem by recomputing eligible scientific routes after every executed step and evaluating the resulting artifact, the validity of the committed route, and the justification of any abstention.

7 Conclusion

We introduced state-dependent scientific route selection and HazardWeaver, which grounds applicability in literature evidence, composes models and tools through typed capability relations, and updates eligible workflows as analysis evolves. On 141 sealed instances spanning seven single-hazard domains and four multi-hazard classes, HazardWeaver achieves 89.4% DCA versus 41.1% for the strongest baseline, with the largest gains on multiple-route tasks. Ablations and evaluation across five backbones confirm the contributions and transferability of its route-selection architecture.

Appendix

Appendix A HWB Scope and Benchmark Construction

This appendix provides the benchmark composition, implementation details, baseline adaptations, evaluation protocol, and supplementary results supporting the main paper. All reported results use the same sealed 141-instance inventory and the DCA evaluator.

A.1 Benchmark Scope

HWB contains 141 sealed instances spanning seven single-hazard domains and four multi-hazard interaction classes. The final inventory contains 90 single-hazard and 51 multi-hazard instances. At the initial state, 45 instances admit one registered route and 96 expose multiple candidate routes.

The construction infrastructure begins from a global atlas of 3,062 registered geospatial scenarios, of which 542 were materialized for benchmark generation. The atlas is a construction resource: headline results are computed exclusively on the sealed 141-instance inventory. The selected instances preserve the diversity of their scientific sources while binding every task to an explicit output contract, candidate route set, capability state, and task-native evaluator.

The eleven source families provide observed events, forcing variables, operational products, and reference outputs for benchmark construction. They support wildfire, flood, landslide, earthquake, tropical-cyclone, drought, heatwave, and multi-hazard tasks across geographically diverse settings.

A.2 Hazard and Route Strata

The hazard-composition and route-multiplicity strata are independent. Figure A.2 reports their joint distribution, allowing performance to be examined both by scientific composition and by the amount of route choice presented to the agent. Multiple-route cases occur in both single- and multi-hazard settings.

Each instance specifies a scientific target, initial state, information cutoff, candidate route set, capability state, output contract, and task-native evaluator. The 96 multiple-route instances expose more than one registered candidate at the initial state. The evaluator checks the committed route against the benchmark-side criterion bound to the corresponding scenario.

A.3 Construction and Sealing

Benchmark construction proceeds through four stages. First, scientific datasets and operational products are mapped to task definitions with explicit output variables, units, spatial and temporal support, and evaluation criteria. Second, candidate route families are instantiated from Route Cards and executable capabilities. Third, every candidate instance undergoes schema, provenance, temporal-cutoff, and replay checks. Finally, the selected inventory, route registry, capability versions, evaluator contracts, and reference artifacts are frozen together.

Every sealed instance has at least one construction-time workflow that can produce the required artifact in a clean environment. This workflow establishes solvability during construction; it is not shown to the evaluated agent and does not prescribe its execution trajectory.

Appendix B Route Cards, Capabilities, and Agent Operations

B.1 Route Card Representation

A Route Card records the scientific and executable information required to determine whether a route is applicable and realizable. Its principal fields are summarized in Table B.1. Full HazardWeaver resolves the frozen HKC-derived conditions associated with these Route Cards at the initial state and revisits their status when permitted evidence changes. The HKC-off condition in RQ2 removes this evidence-linked applicability layer while retaining the remainder of the evaluation pipeline.

B.2 Typed Capability Representation

HCG contains 82 registered capability specifications corresponding to 79 distinct executable capabilities. Capabilities include scientific datasets, empirical equations, numerical models, learned models, simulators, transformations, and coupling operators. Each input and output port records the scientific variable, unit, representation, spatial and temporal support, resolution, uncertainty metadata, and provenance requirements. Representation-preserving transfers may connect capabilities directly. Operations that change information, including interpolation, aggregation, thresholding, learned downscaling, and unit conversion, remain explicit capabilities. Their effects therefore remain visible in the executed workflow and its provenance record.

B.3 Permitted Agent Operations

Table B.2 lists the grounded operations used by HWA. Every operation either inspects the current state, executes a registered capability, or produces an auditable state transition.

Appendix C Evaluation and Reporting Protocol

C.1 Decision-Constrained Accuracy

DCA follows Eq. 8 in the main paper. For an artifact submission, a pass requires task-native artifact success together with benchmark-side route validity, provenance validity, typed and causal execution validity, and the applicable resource contract. An abstention is credited only under the registered recovery criterion in Eq. 7. Missing, incomplete, or unevaluated submissions remain in the denominator and count as failures.

For reporting, EqE_{q} denotes the artifact-validity factor in Eq. 8, while VqV_{q} aggregates the corresponding trajectory-validity factors. Table 3 reports their marginal pass rates; headline DCA requires them jointly with benchmark-side route validity. Consequently, EqE_{q} or VqV_{q} may exceed DCA when the remaining criterion is not satisfied.

C.2 Task-Native Evaluators

HWB preserves the scientific evaluator appropriate to each output rather than forcing heterogeneous artifacts into a common numerical error. Table C.1 summarizes the evaluator families. Exact thresholds, output fields, and units are stored with the sealed instance contracts.

C.3 Statistical Reporting

Instance-level proportions use Wilson 95% confidence intervals. Macro DCA is the unweighted mean of the 11 track-level DCA rates; its 95% interval is obtained by resampling the 11 tracks with replacement for 5,000 bootstrap replicates using seed 42. Comparisons between HazardWeaver and individual baselines use an exact paired McNemar test over the same 141 sealed instances.

Appendix D Implementation Details

D.1 Language-Model Backbones

Experiments use seed 11, temperature 0.2, the frozen HKC registry, the matched execution protocol, and DCA rescoring. All compared methods operate on the same sealed inventory, candidate route catalog, scientific execution interface, evaluator contracts, and per-instance failure policy. A run that does not return a valid scored submission counts as a failure.

D.2 Execution Records

Each run stores the selected route, route commitments, capability invocations, generated artifacts, provenance edges, state transitions, and terminal submission. Numerical, spatial, and probabilistic outputs are generated by registered scientific capabilities; the policy model controls route selection and execution flow.

Appendix E Baseline Adaptations

The source systems target different execution environments and task types. We therefore adapt their published decision principles to the common HWB route-selection interface. Every method receives the same task description, candidate Route Cards, registered capability identifiers, public output requirements, and scientific execution interface. After route selection, the chosen route is executed and evaluated through the same sealed replay and DCA stack used for HazardWeaver.

The adaptations preserve the characteristic control strategy of each method while avoiding method-specific scientific tools, private reference artifacts, or evaluator feedback during route selection. Table E.1 summarizes the resulting implementations.

These adaptations separate route-selection strategy from scientific execution. Their outputs remain fully comparable because the selected capabilities are evaluated on the same instances with the same artifact and route contracts.

Appendix F Supplementary Experimental Results

F.1 Exact RQ2 Ablation Results

Table F.1 gives the counts underlying Figure 3. The 96 instances are the multiple-route stratum of the sealed 141-instance benchmark. Removing either evidence-linked applicability conditions or typed capability composition reduces DCA for every backbone.

The route-update ablation in Table 2 uses 40 applicable instances drawn from the sealed pool. Across five backbones, updated eligibility passes 83 of 200 evaluated backbone–cell combinations, compared with 32 of 200 under fixed initial eligibility. This pooled value is descriptive; the per-backbone comparisons remain the primary result.

F.2 Paired Significance Tests

The test is paired at the instance level: for each baseline, HWA-only counts cases solved exclusively by HazardWeaver, whereas BL-only counts cases solved exclusively by that baseline. This construction controls for variation in task difficulty because both systems are evaluated on exactly the same 141 instances. The imbalance is substantial for every comparison. Even against Plan-and-Solve, the strongest baseline by aggregate DCA, HazardWeaver uniquely solves 75 instances while losing only seven in the opposite direction. The pattern becomes still more pronounced for the shared-tool controllers; for example, HazardWeaver records 84 unique successes against ReAct with no ReAct-only success. All exact McNemar tests remain significant by a wide margin.

These paired results complement the aggregate comparison in Table 1. The advantage is not produced by averaging over a small number of unusually favorable tracks or by one isolated family of tasks. Instead, the discordant outcomes consistently favor HazardWeaver across the sealed inventory and across baseline designs based on planning, reflection, retrieval, iterative refinement, and sampled agreement. This provides instance-level evidence that explicit scientific route eligibility improves the reliability of the resulting decisions beyond the particular control strategy used for comparison.

F.3 Joint Hazard and Route Strata

Figure F.2 separates hazard composition from route multiplicity instead of treating either property as a proxy for the other. HazardWeaver performs strongly in both route-rich strata, solving 58 of 61 single-hazard and 32 of 35 multi-hazard instances with multiple candidate routes. Its advantage is therefore preserved when route choice is combined with a composed scientific analysis. Plan-and-Solve is competitive on the smaller multi-hazard, one-route subset, where it solves 13 of 16 instances compared with 12 for HazardWeaver. This local result also shows that the overall comparison is not uniformly favorable by construction. The largest separation appears once the task requires choosing among several routes. Plan-and-Solve falls from 13 of 16 on multi-hazard, one-route tasks to eight of 35 on the corresponding multiple-route stratum, whereas HazardWeaver solves 32 of those 35 instances. AIDE shows a similar difference between the route regimes. Together with the controlled ablations in RQ2, this stratification supports that HazardWeaver’s principal advantage lies in organizing scientific route choice while retaining strong execution across both isolated and composed hazard analyses.

F.4 Track-Level Cross-Backbone Results

Performance is distributed across all 11 tracks. The tropical-cyclone trajectory track is solved by every backbone, while the dynamic flood inundation track remains a shared bottleneck. The multi-hazard tracks produce greater cross-backbone separation, consistent with the broader profiles shown in Figure 4(c).

Appendix G Benchmark Sealing and Quality Control

G.1 Evaluator Validation

Before sealing, the evaluator was exercised on 160 controlled fixtures spanning eight decision classes: valid alternative execution, scientifically inapplicable route, capability-incompatible route, justified abstention, unjustified abstention, post-cutoff information use, prediction without capability provenance, and coupling-insensitive multi-hazard output. All 160 fixtures produced their expected accept or reject decision.

G.2 Information Separation

Reference artifacts, evaluator thresholds beyond the public task specification, construction-time workflows, and benchmark-side route judgments are held outside the solver context. Agents receive the task, initial state, candidate route descriptions, permitted capabilities, and public output requirements. Evaluation is performed only after terminal submission. All benchmark-side route judgments are frozen before any evaluated policy run; evaluation never derives or revises its route criterion from the tested system’s output.

G.3 Route-Registry Review

We conducted a stratified human review of 86 route–condition pairs drawn from 44 benchmark cells across all 11 tracks. All 27 sampled witness routes were judged scientifically applicable. Candidates rejected by the sealed contract were subsequently adjudicated against the requested output, scientific semantics, and capability requirements; this review found no route that was both contract-valid and omitted from the registry. We use this review as quality control for the sealing procedure rather than as a claim that the catalog exhausts every route that future scientific work may establish.

Appendix H Representative Execution Traces

H.1 Route Revision After an Execution-State Change

In a representative seismic instance, HWA initially enumerates the available seismic routes, commits to the capability satisfying the phase-picking contract, and begins execution. An intermediate state change invalidates the current realization. HWA updates the capability state, reinstantiates a compatible realization, recommits under the revised state, and completes the required artifact. The final route and phase-picking output both satisfy the sealed evaluator.

This trace illustrates the distinction between retaining a scientific route family and repairing its executable realization: the scientific target remains appropriate, while the capability path must be reconstructed from the updated state.

H.2 Failure Under an Incomplete Cascade

A representative post-fire debris-flow cascade failure occurs when the policy selects a debris-flow volume route for a task requiring the complete burn–rainfall–debris-flow cascade. The selected capability produces a scientifically meaningful intermediate quantity but does not satisfy the terminal route and output contract. The evaluator therefore rejects the submission. This case shows that successful execution of an individual scientific model does not by itself establish a decision-valid multi-stage analysis.

Appendix I Reproducibility and Release Contents

The release is organized around the sealed inventory so that every reported aggregate can be reconstructed from per-instance records. Table I.1 summarizes the principal artifacts.

A complete reproduction first materializes the frozen task and capability versions, executes the selected system configuration on all 141 instances, applies the sealed evaluator to each terminal record, and then aggregates the resulting per-instance decisions. The released table inputs provide an additional direct check that the manuscript values match the sealed evaluation outputs.

Appendix J Limitations

HazardWeaver operates within a frozen scientific capability catalog and evidence index. HKC conditions reflect the literature corpus and Route Cards available at benchmark construction; new evidence, revised standards, or updated models may require recompilation and review. HWB evaluates artifacts and committed routes through frozen task-specific contracts, so reported validity denotes reproducible agreement with these documented criteria. Headline scoring covers routes registered when the benchmark is sealed; newly established routes require catalog extension and resealing. The 141 instances span eleven hazard tracks and diverse geographic settings without exhausting every event, region, sensor configuration, or operational constraint. Operational forecasting and emergency decision-making therefore require updated evidence, local calibration, and domain review.
